A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LookWhere research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, segmentation, computational-efficiency, and ablation results for LookWhere, including ImageNet, ADE20K, Traffic Signs, and CUB.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Billiards, aerial-image and chest-X-ray evaluations, adversarial tests, and teacher and selector studies.

M1.justification: v2 adds a CNN-selector variant initialized from EfficientNetV2 and a Franca-teacher variant whose selector distills last-layer CLS-token attention. These extend the implemented architecture and supervision choices; the original selector-extractor procedure and three distillation losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Billiard Balls, requiring reasoning about the left-most and right-most numbered objects; AID aerial-scene classification; and NIH Chest X-ray classification across 14 labels. It also evaluates adversarially perturbed ImageNet images. These substantially expand task, domain, and input-condition coverage beyond v1.

E2.justification: The corresponding ImageNet, ADE20K, Traffic Signs, and CUB comparisons retain their baseline memberships in Tables 1–4. Billiards reuses existing comparison methods, while AID and NIH use the already-established DINOv2 baseline. Franca and EfficientNetV2 appear as LookWhere variants rather than new independent competitors.

E3.justification: v2 introduces protocols including AID's 50/50 split, NIH's 10-epoch AUC-ROC evaluation, and AutoAttack on 10K ImageNet images at L-infinity budgets of 1/255 and 0.5/255. Table 4 also marks larger-k CUB models as pretrained with a 256–512 patch range, whereas v1 reports the general 16–128 range. These are added protocols and a reported setting revision, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds adversarial-robustness tests, Franca-teacher experiments and teacher-attention comparisons, selector-layer initialization ablations, and a CNN-selector study. Billiards also gains a random-selection control. These test robustness, dependence on the teacher and architecture, and selection for inter-patch reasoning; the original ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or formal significance tests. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark and analysis results, including Billiards accuracy of 97.3% versus DINOv2's 97.6% in Table 5. Table 4 replaces CUB k=273 accuracy of 89.8% with 90.1% under the newly specified wider pretraining range, revises reported training FLOPs from 19 to 79G, and adds k=684 and Franca entries. This is not evidence of a same-setting accuracy gain.

T1.justification: The mathematical description of tokenization, representations, attention distillation, losses, and interpolation is retained. Neither version adds formal propositions or proofs; the new architectural discussion and empirical metrics do not introduce substantive mathematical developments.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: selector-extractor adaptive computation, joint what-where distillation, transferable selection, and efficient recognition. The headline efficiency claims remain unchanged; the additional experiments primarily supply new supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 interprets alternative-teacher and CNN-selector results as evidence of broader applicability and discusses initialization sensitivity at small patch budgets. It explicitly limits the adversarial findings to weak attacks without claiming practical robustness. The original limitations concerning a frozen selector and exclusively spatial computation remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies dataset sizes, splits, image resolutions, batch sizes, and training budgets for the added evaluations, plus attack settings and alternative teacher/selector initialization information. Table 4 discloses the wider CUB pretraining patch range. Existing implementation guidance, profiling hardware, and code-and-weights access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting token-reduction context, AutoAttack, Franca, AID, chest-X-ray evaluation, and EfficientNetV2. The substantive positioning against token reduction, token selection, LTRP, and earlier attention-distillation work remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are retained, with localized wording edits, added experimental subsections, and affiliation/header updates. The appendix heading 'Extractor Input Size and Depth' becomes 'Selector Input Size and Depth,' correcting its mismatch with the existing main-text description rather than changing the experiment.

P2.justification: Figure 4 expands from two to three benchmark panels. v2 adds teacher-attention illustrations, Billiards selector examples, and benchmark, initialization, and architecture tables; Tables 3–4 gain dual-teacher entries and explanatory footnotes. The original attention heatmaps and selector examples are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central generality claim, which v1 tested with DINOv2-based ViT models on its original benchmarks. Billiards, aerial and medical evaluations, and alternative teacher/selector studies test previously unsupported task, domain, and architectural extensions. They also expose teacher-dependent and accuracy-versus-computation tradeoffs. The original evidence is preserved and adversarial claims are explicitly qualified, although statistical uncertainty remains unreported.
